title: How Cozey turns its operators into software builders on Vercel
description: Employees outside engineering, including warehouse, finance, and support staff, are now building applications and deploying them to Vercel Finance uses an app it built to review profit and loss weekly instead of monthly Adopting Vercel Flags allowed Cozey to retire a separate tool that cost approximately $80,000 annually Six projects, including the storefront, use AI Gateway Cozey is a Canadian furniture company that makes modular sofas customers can configure for their homes. It runs its storefront and most of its back-office applications on Vercel. Warehouse, finance, and customer support employees now securely deploy their own apps on that same platform. Turning everyday problems into working applications CEO Fred Aubé encourages employees to solve problems they encounter without waiting for another team to take them on. Sam Morrison, VP of Digital, saw teams reach the limits of what they could prototype in an AI chat. Employees used coding agents to build web apps. With Vercel, they could deploy an app themselves and give coworkers a link to a working tool. In the warehouse, a coordinator built a live floor plan that shows where boxes sit and what staff are doing. Sam says engineering would not have prioritized that project. Finance built its own app to track profit and loss and now uses it to review performance every week instead of once a month. A customer support representative built an app that uses AI to generate images of Cozey furniture in a customer’s own room. In October, Cozey planned to make the tool available to shoppers. Sam says a new app appears almost every week. Extending Vercel from the storefront to the business behind it Sam estimates that the Atmosphere sofa collection alone has about 1.2 million possible configurations. Cozey worked with an agency specializing in Next.js to rebuild its storefront on Vercel. With a custom front end, the team could decide how shoppers explore those options. Cozey uses Fluid compute for functions on the storefront. It runs internal Python backends and the Cozey Operating System, or C.O.S., on Vercel. Teams use C.O.S. to forecast orders, manage warehouse and retail operations, review finances, and track business performance. Operating margin depends in part on how quickly furniture moves from incoming containers to customer shipments. Each C.O.S. pull request gets a Vercel Preview Deployment , giving the team a working application to test before release. Cozey’s engineers reported that with caching, builds on Vercel took a couple of minutes. They also share preview links with Fred so he can try changes and give feedback. The team uses Vercel Flags to control how new features reach users, replacing a separate tool that cost approximately $80,000 annually. After release, performance metrics on Vercel give the team a common reference for checking how applications are running. When Cozey launched in Australia, the team had regional backend work to do. For the storefront on Vercel, Sam says, “it wasn’t even a conversation.” Managing access as more people build As more employees began building, Cozey needed to manage who could open their applications and who could deploy and maintain them. An employee once deployed an app that anyone on the internet could open. For internal apps that had shipped without appropriate authentication, Sam turned on access protection on Vercel . “It saved us from some pretty serious privacy risks,” says Sam. Cozey uses single sign-on so members of its Vercel team can sign in with company credentials. The company manages team membership through groups in its employee directory with Directory Sync . Giving AI applications a common way to access models As more teams built with AI, Sam saw them repeating the work of connecting to models. Six Cozey projects, including the storefront, send model requests through Vercel AI Gateway . Cozey’s engineers use it to call models from their code editors, too. Sam wants all of Cozey’s model requests to go through Gateway. AI Gateway gives teams one interface for different model providers. If a provider is unavailable, the gateway can route the request to another provider that serves the same model. It adds no markup to provider token prices. Sam describes the added cost of routing requests through it as “basically $0 in additional overhead.” The company is also developing what it calls the Agentic Mesh, a system to coordinate AI use across internal applications and customer experiences. The coordinating service is being built on AWS, with AI Gateway planned for model requests and Vercel for application deployment. It is intended to help teams decide which models to use and where to run applications, while giving engineering visibility into AI usage and costs. What's next Sam says engineering wouldn’t have prioritized a live map of the warehouse floor. The coordinator who needed to see where the boxes were could make a different call, build the map, and share it with the people moving them. When the digital team sees an idea worth taking further, it has a working app to build on. Cozey chose a custom storefront on Vercel so it could decide how shoppers explore its furniture. Sam’s next goal is for employees outside engineering to share that control. If shoppers keep asking the same question about a sofa, the support rep who hears it could put the answer on the product page. Read more

title: Workflow is 10x faster, again
description: Workflow SDK 5.8 runs workflows on a new execution engine, rebuilt for performance. Step-to-step latency is 12x lower, and large fan-outs, like running 256 steps in parallel, use 14x less function time outside your step code. This directly improves turn times for durable AI agents , among many other improvements. To get the new engine, upgrade to workflow@5.8.0 or later. New runs will use the new engine by default, and runs already started on an older version will safely keep running on that version. Make sure your steps are idempotent where possible to get the most out of this upgrade. Drastically reduced overhead In our benchmarks comparing 5.2.0 to 5.8.0 , p75 step-to-step overhead fell from 85 ms to 7 ms. The median run, including 102 seconds of step work, finished in 111 seconds instead of 3.0 minutes. Running 256 parallel steps in a fan-out added 5.5× less overhead, 2.5 seconds instead of 13.5 seconds, and the median run spent 14× less time in functions beyond the steps' own work, 105 seconds instead of 1,446. A five-turn agent loop that streams its tokens through durable streams and calls tools added 0.9 seconds of overhead instead of 3.0 seconds, 3.3× less. Consult the benchmarks page for how we measure these numbers. Resuming after 1 second idle time went from 425 ms to 184 ms, 2.3× faster. Resumptions more than 5 seconds out might see slightly larger overhead. You can choose to keep functions warm for longer to optimize time-to-resume at the cost of additional compute time. Speculative execution for retryable steps Many of the above benefits rely on speculative execution of Steps. Only Steps that are idempotent can be run in this way. A step that passes its stepId as an idempotency key , like the Stripe charge below, is already safe and needs no changes. If your step is sensitive and can't be retried, mark it with maxRetries = 0 to opt out and ensure it still runs at most once. You should already be making Steps idempotent wherever possible, or flag them with maxRetries = 0 , to ensure Workflow SDK doesn't re-run your Steps when it's not safe to do so. Get started Upgrade to workflow@5.8.0 . To keep creating runs on the previous engine after upgrading, set WORKFLOW_SPEC_VERSION=8 . If you're on 4.x, start with the upgrade guide , since v5 is a major release. Using a third-party World? All Worlds maintained by Vercel already support the new engine. A third-party World needs to support World spec version 9 before upgrading gives you any of these improvements. Until it does, new runs keep using the previous engine. Read more

title: Delete a run's data on demand in Workflow SDK
description: The Workflow SDK now lets you delete a finished run's stored data on demand. This feature gives you the ability to quickly meet compliance and security requirements when sensitive data needs to be purged from run payloads. Deleting a run's data deletes any inputs, outputs, hook payloads, and error traces for the run and its related entities. This does not delete the run's metadata : the run is still listed in observability. Attributes, hook tokens, and timings for steps and events can still be inspected. You can delete a run's data from the Vercel Dashboard, or via the CLI: You can also delete a run's data programmatically from your code: Deletion applies to finished runs only, so a run that is still going is skipped and keeps running. If you want to delete a run's payload as soon as it finishes, use the retention settings instead. Upgrade to workflow@5.7.0 or higher to use this feature. Learn more in the deleteRuns() reference . Read more

title: Inkling 2 Mini now available on AI Gateway
description: Inkling 2 Mini from Thinking Machines is now available on AI Gateway. The small multimodal reasoning model is built for agentic coding, tool use, and knowledge work, with text and image inputs and text output. Inkling 2 Mini has 26.4 billion total parameters and 3.4 billion active per token. The model runs its middle layers more than once for every token, which lets it reason further before writing anything down and often reach an answer with fewer reasoning tokens. Like Inkling 2 Small, it is strongest on long-running agentic tasks. The model has a 1M-token context window, and reasoning effort can be set from none through max . Use thinkingmachines/inkling-2-mini as the model name: To use it in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup: Then select thinkingmachines/inkling-2-mini in the agent. See the coding agents guide for details. Try Inkling 2 Mini in the model playground . AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting , Zero Data Retention support , budgets for API keys , routing rules , and more. AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and does not charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests. You can view all language models available on AI Gateway. Read more
